title: Seeing the picture before you take it
teaches: Backgrounds, light direction, framing and fieldcraft: the decisions made with your feet before any dial is turned

blocks.text: **The challenge.** A mule deer steps out of the trees into a meadow forty metres away and stops, ears up, looking straight at you.[^mule-deer] You have perhaps half a minute. There are two quite different pictures here. One is a portrait: the deer large, sharp and bright against the dark wall of the forest, nothing else in the frame. The other is the deer in its place: small, standing in the gold grass with open hills rolling away behind it. Both are good. What you should not get is the picture in between, with the forest edge running straight down through the deer's back.

blocks.caption: The same deer from 40 m: a portrait against the forest, and the deer in its place

blocks.text: The two pictures were taken with nearly the same settings. The differences are where the photographer stood, sixteen metres apart, and how far they zoomed. Neither is a dial on the camera, and neither can be fixed afterwards.

parts.title: The background is half the picture

blocks.text: When you look at an animal, your attention locks onto it and you hardly see what is behind it. The camera sees everything equally. A bright patch of sky through the trees, a fence post growing out of the deer's head, a road sign, the forest edge cutting through its back: these are invisible in the field and glaring in the picture. Before pressing the shutter, look past the subject, at the edges of the frame and at what is directly behind it.

You change the background by moving. Step sideways and, seen past the subject, things just behind it hardly shift while things far behind it slide a long way; this is **parallax**,[^parallax] the same effect that makes fence posts race past a train window while far hills hardly move. With a deer at forty metres and a forest edge sixty metres beyond it, each metre you step moves the edge sixty centimetres across behind the deer. The sixteen metres between the two pictures at the start moved it almost ten metres: the whole difference between the two backgrounds.

blocks.caption: A deer 40 m away, a forest edge 60 m behind it, and open hills far off
blocks.task: Put the deer against dark forest, zoomed to a portrait of 400 mm or more

blocks.text: Zooming changes the background too, in a different way: it decides how much of it the frame takes in. At the wide end you get the forest, the hills and the meadow all at once; zoomed in, a few square metres of forest. Then the aperture and the distances decide how blurred that piece is, as in the lesson The aperture and what stays sharp. A good background is usually even in tone, darker or lighter than the subject, and far enough behind it to blur.

Walking around a subject also changes the light on it, as much as the time of day does. With the sun behind you the subject is evenly lit, every feather clear, and a small bright reflection of the sun, the **catchlight**, appears in its eye. An animal's eye without a catchlight looks dull and lifeless in a picture.

blocks.caption: A bird on a branch, with the sun moved around it
blocks.task: Try front light, side light and back light

blocks.text: Front light is the safe choice and often a flat one. Side light, with the sun at ninety degrees, gives shape and shows texture, fur, bark and feathers in relief, but half the subject falls into shadow, which is harder to expose. Back light is the dramatic one, and the hardest: decide whether you are exposing for the glowing rim or the subject's face, as in the lesson The colour of light. With a still subject you can often choose by walking a quarter circle around it, slowly.

Decide which picture you are making, because they want different things. A **portrait** is about the animal: fill a good part of the frame, keep the background plain and soft, and get the eye sharp. A **place** picture is about the animal in its world: let it be small, make sure it is still clearly the subject (against a plain patch, or in the light), and give the landscape room. The picture in between, a medium-sized animal against a busy medium-sharp background, rarely works.

A few habits help either way. **Get down to its level**: an animal photographed from standing height, looking down, looks small and distant; at its eye level it looks like a creature with a life. **Leave room in the direction it faces**, so it has somewhere to look or move into. **Keep the horizon level** and out of its neck. And **check the edges of the frame** before you press: a stray branch tip or a bright corner pulls the eye away.

Getting close is a skill of its own, called fieldcraft. A long lens lets you stay well back: an animal that is relaxed, feeding or resting makes a better picture than one staring at you, about to run. Approach slowly and at an angle rather than straight on, keep low, stop often, and move while it is busy feeding or looking away. A car often works as a hide; many animals ignore a vehicle but flee from a person stepping out.

If an animal stops what it was doing to watch you, you are close enough; if it moves away, you were too close. Never flush a bird (startle it into flying) for a flight shot, and keep well away from nests and dens, especially in spring.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Look past the subject to the background and the edges of the frame before you press.
Stepping sideways slides far backgrounds across behind a subject much more than near ones: parallax.
Walk around the subject to choose between front, side and back light.
Make either a close portrait on a plain background or a wide picture of the animal in its place.
Get down to eye level, leave room in front, and stay far enough back that it carries on.

items.question: In your picture a fence post seems to grow out of a heron's head. What is the quickest fix in the field?
options: Step a little to one side
Use a wider aperture
Raise the ISO
Switch to continuous autofocus
items.why: Moving sideways slides the background across behind the heron, so the post moves away from its head. A wider aperture would soften the post but leave it there.

items.question: You step two metres to your right. Which moves farther across behind a deer: a bush 2 m behind it or a forest 60 m behind it?
options: The forest
The bush
Both move the same distance
Neither moves
items.why: This is parallax. Things far behind the subject slide across behind it much more than things close to it.

items.question: What is a catchlight?
options: The light source reflected in an animal's eye
A small flash fired to fill in the shadows
The bright edge around a backlit subject
A highlight that has lost all of its detail
items.why: A catchlight is the small reflection of the sun or sky in the eye. Without it, an eye in a photo tends to look flat and dead.

items.question: Which light shows the texture of bark and fur most strongly?
options: Side light
Front light
Overcast light
Light from directly overhead
items.why: Light skimming across a surface from the side throws tiny shadows from every ridge and hair, which shows texture. Front light fills those shadows in.

items.question: Why photograph a fox from low down rather than standing?
options: At its eye level it looks like a creature with a life
The light is always better close to the ground
The camera focuses faster when it is held low
It makes the fox appear much larger in the frame
items.why: Shooting down makes an animal look small and seen from outside its world. At eye level, the viewer meets it as an equal, and the background is farther away and softer too.

items.question: A heron you are approaching stops fishing and stares at you. What should you do?
options: Stop, or back off, and let it settle
Move faster before it flies
Make a noise so it looks up for the photo
Get the shot quickly with the flash
items.why: A change in behaviour means you are close enough. Pushing closer will flush it, and a relaxed, fishing heron is the better picture anyway.

summary: **The camera sees everything.** Look behind the subject and around the edges before you press.
**Move to move the background.** Stepping sideways slides far things across behind the subject much more than near ones: parallax.
**Zoom decides how much background; aperture and distance decide how soft.** Even, darker or lighter, and far behind is best.
**Walk around for the light.** Front light gives a catchlight, side light shape, back light an outline.
**Choose portrait or place.** A big animal on a plain background, or a small one in its landscape, not halfway.
**Get to eye level and leave room in front.** Keep horizons level and out of necks.
**Get close without disturbing.** Approach slowly, stop when the animal notices, and never flush it for a picture.

mule-deer.title: Ears like a mule
mule-deer.text: Mule deer are named for their large ears. They are common across western North America and often pause to look back before fleeing, which gives photographers their chance.

parallax.title: Parallax, in numbers
parallax.text: Step a distance s sideways while keeping your camera on a subject D away. Something a further B behind the subject shifts across behind it by s × B ÷ (D + B), measured at the subject. With D = 40 m and B = 60 m, that is 0.6 m per metre stepped; for a bush only 2 m behind it would be 5 cm. Astronomers use the same geometry, with the Earth's orbit as the step, to measure the distances to nearby stars.
